(The following is an unofficial English translation of the Monetary Policy Direction for
The 'Monetary Policy Direction for 2013' is published in accordance with the provisions of Article 6 of the Bank of Korea Act, upon resolution by the Monetary Policy Committee.
Article 6 (Setting Monetary Policy Directions)
(1) The Bank of Korea shall set an inflation target in consultation with
(2) The Bank of Korea shall set and publish its monetary policy direction every year.
(3) The Bank of Korea shall do its best to achieve the inflation target as provided for in paragraph (1).
The inflation target for the 2013-15 period is set at 2.5-3.5% in terms of the rate of increase in consumer prices.

The target has been changed to this range from the previous 3.0±1%, in overall consideration of the recent trend of price stabilization, the medium-term inflation forecast and the enhanced accountability of the central bank for price stability.

By lowering the upper bound of the target from 4.0% to 3.5% in addition to narrowing its range, the Bank of Korea seeks to establish a foundation for price stability at the level of advanced countries.
The Bank also publishes a comprehensive report on inflation twice a year, explaining its trend, background, future outlook and conditions, the monetary policy direction, and so on.

During 2013 the global economy is forecast to show a recovery, albeit at a moderate pace, boosted chiefly by major countries' support for economic recovery including through monetary policy easing and by the efforts to resolve the euro area fiscal crisis.
Major international organizations such as the IMF expect world economic growth for 2013 to rise somewhat above that in 2012.
The downside risks to growth will still be large, however, due mostly to the euro area fiscal crisis and the fiscal consolidation issue in the
The domestic economy is expected to show a trend of mild recovery, but given the slow pace of recovery in growth, the output gap is forecast to stay negative.
The growth rate of the domestic economy is projected to gradually increase from the middle of next year, on the back primarily of the global economic recovery.

The output gap is forecast to remain negative given the measured pace of recovery, however, and the uncertainties concerning the future growth path will run high due mostly to the euro area fiscal crisis.
Despite for instance the dampening of the price decline effect credited to institutional factors such as free childcare and school meal
provision, the upward pressures on consumer prices are not expected to be large owing primarily to the easing of demand-side pressures.

The financial markets are likely to remain stable overall, but concerns about volatility expanding exist, due for instance to the euro area fiscal crisis and to advanced countries' quantitative easing policies, and there is a possibility of fund-raising conditions deteriorating for some firms due chiefly to financial institutions' strengthening of risk management.
The household debt problem continues to lurk as a factor causing financial sector vulnerability.

Although the financial markets are likely to remain stable overall, the possibility persists of the volatilities of price variables and foreign investment capital flows expanding, depending largely upon the euro area fiscal crisis, advanced countries' quantitative easing policies and economic conditions in major countries.
The growth in financial institution lending during 2013 is expected to be similar to that in 2012, with overall credit supply conditions exhibiting a generally favorable state.

There is however a likelihood of fund-raising conditions deteriorating for firms whose business conditions are sluggish or whose credit ratings are low, owing for instance to strengthening of risk management by financial institutions and to credit differentiation in the corporate bond markets.
Due in most part to the lack of improvement in household income conditions, it will be hard for the household debt problem to improve

In conducting monetary policy, the Bank, while firmly anchoring the basis for price stability, will closely monitor risk factors and changes in financial and economic conditions at home and abroad, and place emphasis on supporting the economy's recovery of growth.

The Bank will work to enhance financial system stability and respond actively when factors causing financial market instability arise, thereby promoting financial stability.
In addition, it will strengthen its support for small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and other vulnerable sectors.

While firmly anchoring the basis for price stability in operating the Base Rate, the Bank will closely monitor risk factors and changes in financial and economic conditions at home and abroad, and place emphasis on supporting the economy's recovery of growth.

The Bank will for the time being respond with an emphasis on ensuring that the economy's growth potential is not eroded due to its continued low growth, while closely monitoring the evolution of external risk factors such as the euro area fiscal crisis and the consequent changes in financial and economic conditions at home and abroad.

Together with this, while firmly laying the foundation for price stability by for example lowering inflation expectations, the Bank will at the same time be vigilant so that consumer price inflation is kept within the inflation target range over a medium-term horizon.
The Bank will also closely examine the possibility of economic
imbalances within the economy arising from the extended duration of its accommodative monetary policy stance.
The Bank will devise plans for the enhancement of monetary policy effectiveness and the efficient use of policy instruments.

While examining the effectiveness of the current interest rate-based monetary policy framework, the Bank will also make use for instance of micro-level response measures, thereby boosting its efficacy.

It will push ahead with plans for strengthening the function of the 91-day Monetary Stabilization Bond (MSB) yield as a short-term market reference rate, and seek ways of facilitating smooth functioning of the interest rate transmission channel between the short- and the long-term financial markets.
The Bank will closely analyze recent changes in major advanced countries' methods of conducting monetary policy, their effects, and so forth.
It will work to enhance the usability of its short-term liquidity adjustment instruments, through for instance an expansion of its securities borrowing program.
The Bank will broaden its monetary policy communication with financial market participants and the general public.
The descriptive contents of its statement on the 'Monetary Policy Decision' will be continually improved.

In order that the policy signalling effect of the Monetary Policy Report can be strengthened, the Bank will also enrich its content on matters such as the background to the policy decisions and the future direction of policy.
The Bank will constantly examine factors causing financial sector vulnerabilities, and set up a system for early detection and warning of systemic risks.

It will step up the Financial Stability Report's surveillance and early warning functions with respect to macroprudential conditions, and during its joint examinations with the Financial Supervisory Service strengthen its inspections of banks having significant market influence and of vulnerable sectors.

It will develop surveillance indicators and analytical methods for identification of systemic risks, and measure systemic risks in a comprehensive and systematic manner through its newly constructed Systemic Risk Assessment Model for Macroprudential Policy (SAMP).
The Bank will make use of its monetary policy instruments to secure financial system stability.
It will devise ways of utilizing monetary policy instruments capable of curbing the build-up of risk in the financial
The Bank will redouble its efforts to alleviate potentially destabilizing factors in the financial markets such as the household debt problem.

As and when needed, it will in consultation with the government and others draw up measures for instance to improve the household debt structure and lessen the debt servicing burdens of the vulnerable groups.
The Bank will seek smooth transition to global financial regulatory standards.
It will keep an eye on changes in financial institution and market participant attitudes that may appear in the course of transition to BASEL Ⅲ, and devise countermeasures as needed.
It will also support the implementation domestically of the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMIs).
The Bank will prepare thoroughly for the possibility of any
expansion in financial and foreign exchange market volatility resulting for instance from sudden capital in- and outflows, and respond effectively should emergencies occur.

The Bank will conduct constant and close monitoring for instance of the state of capital in- and outflows and movements of price variables, and in the event of an expansion in foreign capital flows due for example to the quantitative easing policies of advance countries, it will in consultation with the government flexibly implement macro-prudential policies for the foreign exchange sector and devise other such market stabilization measures.

It will also continue to review and supplement its comprehensive stage-by-stage Contingency Plan to guard against the possibility of deterioration in market conditions as a result for instance of the euro area fiscal crisis or any heightening of geopolitical risks related to North Korea or the Middle East.
The Bank will align its policy instruments for financial and foreign exchange market stability, and strengthen its cooperation to this end both domestically and internationally.
It will review concrete plans for carrying out its lender of last resort function, the conditions for which have been eased with revision of the Bank of Korea Act.

It will step up its cooperation and information sharing with the government, the supervisory authorities, and other relevant institutions, and strive as well to enhance its financial cooperation with major central banks, international organizations, and so
The Bank will boost the efficiency of its financial support for SMEs through its Aggregate Credit Ceiling Loans.
It will modify this program so that support can be reinforced for instance to sectors whose levels of contribution to employment and growth are high and to vulnerable sectors.
The Bank will work to upgrade the method of operating the program in ways that can increase the incentives for financial institutions to expand their SME lending.
It will regularly carry out surveys on the status of utilization of its support funds and analyses of their performance.
While closely checking the financial and economic situation and SME funding conditions, the Bank will flexibly adjust the ceiling on its Aggregate Credit Ceiling Loans.
